::: {.callout-note .objectives}
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- write `if`, `else if` and `else` blocks and predict which branch runs;
- explain why an `if` condition must be a **single** `TRUE` or `FALSE`, and use `&&`, `||`, `any()` and `all()` accordingly;
- choose between `if`, `ifelse()`, `dplyr::if_else()`, `dplyr::case_when()` and `switch()`;
- validate the inputs of a function with clear error messages.
:::


## 1. Why do programs need to take decisions?

A shop applies a different VAT (value-added tax) rate depending on the product:

| Category | Products | VAT |
|---|---|---|
| A | Books, magazines, newspapers, … | 8% |
| B | Vegetables, meat, beverages, … | 10% |
| C | T-shirts, jeans, trousers, … | 20% |

To compute the final price, the code must **choose** a rate based on the category: *if* the product is in category A, multiply by 1.08; *otherwise, if* it is in B, multiply by 1.10; *otherwise* multiply by 1.20. This lesson shows the tools R offers for such decisions, and when to use each one.

## 2. `if` and `else`

The basic structure is:

```{r}
#| label: if-syntax
#| eval: false
if (condition) {
  # code run when condition is TRUE
} else {
  # code run when condition is FALSE
}
```

![Flow of an `if`/`else` statement: exactly one of the two blocks runs, then the program continues after the whole statement.](../../images/lesson10-img1.png){fig-align="center" width="55%"}

```{r}
#| label: if-example
quantity <- 25

if (quantity > 20) {
  message_text <- "You sold a lot!"
} else {
  message_text <- "Not enough for today."
}
message_text
```

The `else` part is optional: without it, nothing happens when the condition is `FALSE`.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Style
Put `{` on the same line as `if`, and `} else {` on one line. Indent the code inside the braces by two spaces. If `else` starts a new line at the top level of a script, R thinks the `if` statement has already ended and gives an error.
:::

`if` is itself an expression that returns a value, so you can also write:

```{r}
#| label: if-value
message_text <- if (quantity > 20) "You sold a lot!" else "Not enough for today."
message_text
```

## 3. Several branches: `else if`

Use `else if` to check conditions **in order**. R runs the **first** branch whose condition is `TRUE` and skips all the others.

```{r}
#| label: else-if
quantity <- 25

if (quantity < 20) {
  day <- "Not enough for today."
} else if (quantity <= 30) {
  day <- "Average day."
} else {
  day <- "What a great day!"
}
day
```

Because the branches are checked in order, the second condition does not need to repeat `quantity >= 20`: if we reach it, the first condition was already `FALSE`. Writing conditions this way also avoids **gaps**. For example, the pair `quantity < 20` and `quantity > 20 && quantity <= 30` leaves out exactly `quantity == 20`, which would silently fall into the last branch.

## 4. A condition must be one `TRUE` or `FALSE`

`if` takes a decision for **one** situation. Its condition must therefore be a logical vector of **length 1** that is not `NA`. Anything else is an error:

```{r}
#| label: cond-errors
#| error: true
x <- c(5, 30)
if (x > 20) "big"          # length 2: which element decides?

y <- NA
if (y > 20) "big"          # NA: R cannot decide
```

(Since R 4.2 a condition of length > 1 is an error; older versions only warned and used the first element, which hid many bugs.)

### `&&` and `||` versus `&` and `|`

R has two versions of "and" and "or":

| Operator | Works on | Use it in |
|---|---|---|
| `&`, `\|` | whole vectors, element by element | `filter()`, `ifelse()`, indexing |
| `&&`, `\|\|` | single values only | `if ()` and `while ()` conditions |

`&&` and `||` are also **short-circuit** operators: they stop as soon as the answer is known. In `is.numeric(x) && x > 0`, the comparison `x > 0` is never evaluated when `x` is not numeric. Since R 4.3, giving `&&` or `||` a vector of length > 1 is an error:

```{r}
#| label: and-and
#| error: true
x <- c(5, 30)
x > 0 & x < 10             # vectorised: one answer per element
x > 0 && x < 10            # error: && wants single values
```

To turn many `TRUE`/`FALSE` values into one, summarise them explicitly:

```{r}
#| label: any-all
any(x > 20)                # is at least one element > 20?
all(x > 0)                 # are all elements > 0?
isTRUE(NA > 1)             # TRUE only for a single, non-missing TRUE
```

## 5. The VAT example as a function

Let us write the VAT calculation once, as a [function](14-functions.qmd) that works for one product:

```{r}
#| label: vat-if
# Final price of one product, VAT included.
# price:    a single positive number
# category: "A", "B" or "C"
price_with_vat <- function(price, category) {
  if (category == "A") {
    rate <- 0.08
  } else if (category == "B") {
    rate <- 0.10
  } else if (category == "C") {
    rate <- 0.20
  } else {
    stop("Unknown category '", category, "'. Use \"A\", \"B\" or \"C\".",
         call. = FALSE)
  }
  price * (1 + rate)
}

price_with_vat(10, "A")
price_with_vat(10, "C")
```

The last `else` does not silently pick a rate: an unknown category is almost always a typo, so the function **stops** and tells the user what is allowed.

## 6. `switch()`: choosing by name

When the decision is "which of several named options?", `switch()` is shorter than a chain of `else if`. It compares the first argument with the names of the other arguments and returns the matching value. An unnamed last argument is the **default**.

```{r}
#| label: vat-switch
vat_rate <- function(category) {
  switch(category,
    A = 0.08,
    B = 0.10,
    C = 0.20,
    stop("Unknown category '", category, "'.", call. = FALSE)
  )
}

vat_rate("B")
```

If several names share the same result, leave the value empty and R "falls through" to the next one:

```{r}
#| label: switch-fallthrough
food_group <- function(item) {
  switch(item,
    apple = ,
    banana = "fruit",
    carrot = ,
    potato = "vegetable",
    "unknown"
  )
}
food_group("banana")
food_group("pizza")
```

`switch()` is for **one** value, like `if`. Without a default, an unmatched name returns `NULL` invisibly, which can cause confusing errors later — always add a default or a `stop()`.

## 7. Decisions for a whole vector

`if` decides once. Very often, however, you need one decision **per element** — per row of a data frame. For that you need *vectorised* functions.

### `ifelse()` (base R)

```{r}
#| label: ifelse
sales <- c(10, 25, 40, 18)
ifelse(sales > 20, "good", "poor")
```

`ifelse(test, yes, no)` returns, for each element, the value from `yes` where `test` is `TRUE` and from `no` where it is `FALSE`. It has two weaknesses: it **drops attributes** such as dates and factor levels, and it does not complain when `yes` and `no` have different types:

```{r}
#| label: ifelse-dates
d <- ifelse(TRUE, as.Date("2024-03-01"), NA)
d            # a number, not a date!
class(d)
```

### `dplyr::if_else()`: stricter and safer

`if_else()` works like `ifelse()` but **keeps the type** of `true`/`false`, refuses to mix types (e.g. text and numbers), and has a `missing` argument for `NA` conditions.

```{r}
#| label: if-else
sales <- c(10, 25, NA, 18)
if_else(sales > 20, "good", "poor", missing = "not recorded")
if_else(TRUE, as.Date("2024-03-01"), as.Date(NA))
```

### `dplyr::case_when()`: many conditions

For more than two outcomes, `case_when()` is the vectorised version of `if … else if … else`. Each argument is `condition ~ value`; conditions are checked in order and the first `TRUE` wins. `.default` gives the value when no condition is `TRUE`.

```{r}
#| label: case-when
penguins |>
  mutate(size = case_when(
    body_mass < 3500 ~ "small",
    body_mass < 4500 ~ "medium",
    body_mass >= 4500 ~ "large",
    .default = "unknown"          # here: the 2 penguins with missing mass
  )) |>
  count(size)
```

Now the VAT problem for a whole price list:

```{r}
#| label: vat-vector
basket <- tibble(
  item     = c("novel", "tomatoes", "jeans", "newspaper"),
  category = c("A", "B", "C", "A"),
  price    = c(15, 3.5, 60, 2)
)

basket |>
  mutate(
    rate  = case_when(
      category == "A" ~ 0.08,
      category == "B" ~ 0.10,
      category == "C" ~ 0.20
    ),
    total = price * (1 + rate)
  )
```

::: {.callout-tip .read-output}
## How to read this output
Each row received its own rate. A category not listed in `case_when()` (and no `.default`) would get `NA` for `rate` and `total`, which is visible in the result. That is safer than a silent wrong rate.
:::

### Which tool when?

| Situation | Use |
|---|---|
| One decision (one value, e.g. a function argument) | `if` / `else if` / `else` |
| One value, many named options | `switch()` |
| A column, two outcomes | `dplyr::if_else()` (or `ifelse()` for plain vectors) |
| A column, three or more outcomes | `dplyr::case_when()` |

## 8. Validating inputs

Conditionals are the natural tool for checking that a function received sensible inputs (see also [Writing functions](14-functions.qmd#checking-inputs)). A robust version of `price_with_vat()`:

```{r}
#| label: validate
#| error: true
price_with_vat <- function(price, category = c("A", "B", "C")) {
  category <- match.arg(category)           # only allowed values pass
  if (!is.numeric(price) || length(price) != 1 || price < 0) {
    stop("`price` must be a single non-negative number.", call. = FALSE)
  }
  rate <- switch(category, A = 0.08, B = 0.10, C = 0.20)
  price * (1 + rate)
}

price_with_vat(10, "B")
price_with_vat(10, "D")
price_with_vat(-5, "A")
```

- `match.arg()` compares the argument with the vector of allowed values in the definition and stops with a clear message otherwise. If the user gives no value, it takes the **first** one (`"A"` here).
- The `||` chain is evaluated left to right and stops at the first `TRUE`, so `price < 0` is never evaluated for a non-numeric `price`.

::: {.callout-note .deeper collapse="true"}
## Going deeper: warnings, errors and `tryCatch()`
`stop()` signals an **error** (the function ends), `warning()` a **warning** (the function continues, the user is told at the end), `message()` an informational note. A caller can intercept them with `tryCatch(expr, error = function(e) ..., warning = function(w) ...)`, for example to skip a file that fails to load inside a loop. Use this sparingly: catching errors you do not understand hides bugs. See *Advanced R* (2e), chapter "Conditions".
:::

::: {.callout-warning .pitfall}
## Common pitfalls

1. **Using `if` on a vector.** `if (df$age > 18)` is an error since R 4.2. Use `if_else()`/`case_when()` for columns, or `any()`/`all()` if you really need one decision.
2. **Forgetting `NA`.** `if (x > 3)` fails when `x` is `NA`. Handle missing values first (`if (!is.na(x) && x > 3)`) or use `isTRUE()`.
3. **`=` instead of `==`.** `if (x = 3)` is a syntax error; comparison is `==`.
4. **Gaps and overlaps between branches.** Check the boundary values (here, exactly 20 or 30) and let the order of `else if` do the work.
5. **Comparing decimals with `==`.** `0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3` is `FALSE` because of rounding; use `isTRUE(all.equal(a, b))` or a tolerance.
6. **`ifelse()` and dates/factors.** It returns plain numbers; prefer `if_else()`.
:::

## 9. Check your understanding

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q1. What does this code print for `x <- 20`?

```r
if (x < 10) "low" else if (x < 20) "mid" else "high"
```

`"high"`. `20 < 10` and `20 < 20` are both `FALSE`, so the final `else` runs.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q2. Why does `if (c(1, 5) > 3) "yes"` fail, and how would you ask "is any value larger than 3?"

The condition has length 2, but `if` needs a single `TRUE`/`FALSE`. Write `if (any(c(1, 5) > 3)) "yes"`.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q3. You need a new column `pass` equal to `"yes"` when `score >= 18` and `"no"` otherwise. `if` or `if_else()`?

`if_else(score >= 18, "yes", "no")` inside `mutate()`: one decision **per row** needs a vectorised function.
:::

## 10. Exercises

### Interactive (run in your browser)

::: {.exercise}
[★]{.stars} **Exercise 1 — fill the branches.** Complete `grade()` so that a score below 18 returns `"fail"`, a score from 18 to 26 returns `"pass"`, and a score above 26 returns `"merit"`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_15_1
grade <- function(score) {
  if (score < ______) {
    "fail"
  } else if (score <= ______) {
    "pass"
  } else {
    ______
  }
}
grade(15); grade(18); grade(26); grade(30)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_15_1"}
The thresholds are 18 and 26; the last branch returns `"merit"`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_15_1"}
```r
grade <- function(score) {
  if (score < 18) {
    "fail"
  } else if (score <= 26) {
    "pass"
  } else {
    "merit"
  }
}
grade(15); grade(18); grade(26); grade(30)
```
The four calls give `"fail"`, `"pass"`, `"pass"`, `"merit"`. Check the boundaries 18 and 26 explicitly: they are where most bugs hide.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 2 — debug.** The code below is meant to label each car in `mtcars` as `"efficient"` (more than 25 mpg) or `"thirsty"`, but it fails. Fix it with a vectorised function.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_15_2
library(dplyr)
cars2 <- mtcars
if (cars2$mpg > 25) {
  cars2$type <- "efficient"
} else {
  cars2$type <- "thirsty"
}
table(cars2$type)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_15_2"}
`cars2$mpg > 25` has 32 values. Use `if_else(test, true, false)` (or `ifelse()`).
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_15_2"}
```r
cars2 <- mtcars
cars2$type <- if_else(cars2$mpg > 25, "efficient", "thirsty")
table(cars2$type)
```
Six cars have more than 25 mpg. `if` can only take one decision; `if_else()` takes one per element.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 3 — `case_when()` on penguins.** Create a column `bill_shape` that is `"long"` when `bill_len > 45`, `"medium"` when `bill_len > 40`, and `"short"` otherwise, then count penguins by `species` and `bill_shape`. Missing bill lengths should end up as `NA`, not as `"short"`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_15_3
library(dplyr)
penguins |>
  mutate(bill_shape = case_when(
    bill_len > 45 ~ ______,
    bill_len > 40 ~ ______,
    ______ ~ "short"
  )) |>
  count(species, bill_shape)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_15_3"}
If you use `.default = "short"`, the missing values would become `"short"` too. The last condition can be `bill_len <= 40`: it is `NA` for missing values, so no branch matches and the result is `NA`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_15_3"}
```r
penguins |>
  mutate(bill_shape = case_when(
    bill_len > 45 ~ "long",
    bill_len > 40 ~ "medium",
    bill_len <= 40 ~ "short"
  )) |>
  count(species, bill_shape)
```
Adelie penguins are mostly `"short"`, Chinstrap and Gentoo mostly `"long"`. The two birds without a bill measurement appear with `bill_shape = NA`.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★★]{.stars} **Exercise 4 — `switch()` with validation.** Write `summarise_by(x, stat)` that returns the mean, median or standard deviation of `x` (ignoring `NA`s) depending on `stat`, which must be one of `"mean"`, `"median"`, `"sd"`. Use `match.arg()` and `switch()`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_15_4
summarise_by <- function(x, stat = c("mean", "median", "sd")) {
  stat <- ______(stat)
  switch(stat,
    mean   = mean(x, na.rm = TRUE),
    median = ______,
    sd     = ______
  )
}
summarise_by(penguins$flipper_len)
summarise_by(penguins$flipper_len, "sd")
summarise_by(penguins$flipper_len, "mode")   # should give an error
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_15_4"}
`stat <- match.arg(stat)`; the other branches are `median(x, na.rm = TRUE)` and `sd(x, na.rm = TRUE)`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_15_4"}
```r
summarise_by <- function(x, stat = c("mean", "median", "sd")) {
  stat <- match.arg(stat)
  switch(stat,
    mean   = mean(x, na.rm = TRUE),
    median = median(x, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd     = sd(x, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
}
summarise_by(penguins$flipper_len)        # about 200.9 (default: mean)
summarise_by(penguins$flipper_len, "sd")  # about 14.1
```
Without an explicit `stat`, `match.arg()` picks the first allowed value, `"mean"`. `"mode"` is rejected with a message listing the allowed values.
:::
:::

### Practice on your own computer

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 5 — a shipping-cost function.** Write `shipping_cost(weight, express = FALSE)`: parcels up to 1 kg cost 5, up to 5 kg cost 9, heavier ones cost 9 plus 1.5 per kg above 5. Express delivery doubles the price. The function must stop with a clear message if `weight` is not a single positive number. Test it on 0.5, 5, 8 and `-1` kg.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```r
shipping_cost <- function(weight, express = FALSE) {
  if (!is.numeric(weight) || length(weight) != 1 || is.na(weight) ||
      weight <= 0) {
    stop("`weight` must be a single positive number (in kg).", call. = FALSE)
  }
  cost <- if (weight <= 1) {
    5
  } else if (weight <= 5) {
    9
  } else {
    9 + 1.5 * (weight - 5)
  }
  if (express) cost <- 2 * cost
  cost
}
shipping_cost(0.5)                 # 5
shipping_cost(5)                   # 9
shipping_cost(8, express = TRUE)   # 2 * (9 + 4.5) = 27
```
`shipping_cost(-1)` stops with the message. Note that the checks use `||` so that `weight <= 0` is not evaluated when `weight` is, say, text.
:::
:::

## Summary

| Tool | For | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `if` / `else if` / `else` | one decision | `if (x > 0) "pos" else "non-pos"` |
| `&&`, `\|\|` | combining single conditions | `if (!is.na(x) && x > 0)` |
| `any()`, `all()`, `isTRUE()` | turning many values into one | `if (any(x < 0)) stop(...)` |
| `switch()` | one value, named options | `switch(cat, A = 0.08, B = 0.10, 0.20)` |
| `ifelse()` | base vectorised choice | `ifelse(x > 20, "big", "small")` |
| `dplyr::if_else()` | type-safe vectorised choice | `if_else(x > 20, "big", "small")` |
| `dplyr::case_when()` | many conditions on a column | `case_when(x < 1 ~ "a", .default = "b")` |
| `match.arg()`, `stop()` | input validation | `type <- match.arg(type)` |

- `if` needs **one** non-missing `TRUE`/`FALSE`; columns need **vectorised** tools.
- Use `&&`/`||` inside `if`, and `&`/`|` for vectors.
- Branches are checked **in order**; the first `TRUE` wins.
- Stop with a **clear message** on invalid input instead of guessing.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
